20090-the-uncollected-writings-of-thomas:
Thomas De Quincey, famed for his opium tale, left much work uncollected in his lifetime. Volume two of his uncollected writings gathers later essays, with notes by James Hogg. Three pieces deal with Chinese affairs from a tense time. War with China then seemed close, the notes explain in detail.

Those pieces first ran in Titan in February and April 1857. They then came out as a scarce pamphlet of 152 pages. Hogg adds a long preface and clear notes for new readers. The volume suits readers who want De Quincey beyond his best-known book.
21057-the-log-of-the-flying-fish-a-story:
Harry Collingwood's novel of aerial and submarine peril is often counted among the early works of science fiction. A German professor living in London recruits rich, adventurous Englishmen for a bold voyage. Their craft, the Flying Fish, is built from a new material called aetherium.

Because aetherium is both very light and very strong, the vessel can rise into the air and dive deep under the sea. The crew reach the North Pole, find the remains of a Viking ship, and visit Africa and Mount Everest. Young readers of the time got invention, travel, and danger in one tale.
22060-the-young-franc-tireurs-and-their-:
G. A. Henty wrote The Young Franc-Tireurs for boys who liked their history with gunpowder. The story opens as the Franco-Prussian War breaks out in 1870. Henty had seen the franc-tireurs, France's volunteer irregulars, during the war itself. He judged them brave but too often badly led, and his preface says so plainly.

Two young heroes join the irregulars and march for the Vosges. They fight at the tunnel of Saverne, hunt a traitor, and face desperate odds. Henty packs the tale with real places and events from the war. For Victorian schoolboys, such books were history lessons that read like adventure, and Henty was their master.
22484-gardening-indoors-and-under-glass-:
F. F. Rockwell wrote Gardening Indoors and Under Glass in 1911. It is a practical guide to the propagation and care of house plants. Coldframes and the small greenhouse fall under its title's promise.

Rockwell begins with light, the first need of indoor plants. Almost all plants need an abundance of light, flowering or not. Many require sunshine, especially during dull winter days. Without it, stems grow long, lanky, and weak, he warns. Foliage takes a washed-out, semi-transparent look in poor light. Such plants fall easy victims to disease or insect enemies. His plain rules still serve winter gardeners. The book preserves expert house-plant care from before modern grow lights.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAWilsonEdwinP:
Philip Taubman and Jeff Gerth reported for the New York Times, in an article dated October 12, on two former CIA men in a new business. Edwin P. Wilson and Frank E. Terpil had joined a California electronics company to market sensitive American technology abroad.

Wilson and Terpil became the most notorious ex-agents of their generation, accused of selling arms, explosives, and training to Libya's Muammar Gaddafi. Articles like this one caught them at the start of that exposure, still presenting themselves as legitimate exporters. The piece is preserved as early reporting on the Wilson-Terpil enterprise, before the trials made them famous.
